examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Number of Combinations of Objects Chosen From a Group Fewer Than Ten
examples.problem: There are $10$ employees in a company, and $3$ of them are to be selected to form a committee. How many different selections are possible?
examples.worked_solution:
The number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_nC_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!r!}.
$$

There are $10$ employees, so $n=10.$ We want to select $3$ of those employees to form a committee, so we have $r=3.$

Therefore, the number of different ways to form the committee is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{n}{C}_{r} & ={}_{10}{C}_{3} \\  & =\frac{10!}{(10-3)!3!} \\  & =\frac{10!}{7!3!} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 9\cdot 8\cdot \cancel{7!}}{\cancel{7!}3!} \\  & =\frac{720}{6} \\  & =120.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, note that $(\frac{5}{1})$ means the same thing as ${}_{5}{C}_{1}.$

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=5$ and $r=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{5}{C}_{1} & =\frac{5!}{(5-1)!1!} \\  & =\frac{5!}{4!1!} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot \cancel{4!}}{\cancel{4!}\cdot 1} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$
